me.name: Brylie Wilson
bio: I’m in my element at the start of a project, working out what the problem actually is.

I research the whole system around a brief, including the people, culture, platforms, social context and politics involved, then translate it into a strategy and something people can see and use. That might be editorial, a campaign, an installation or a digital experience, whichever medium suits the concept best.
I’m drawn to small, values‑aligned teams, non‑profits, community organisations and civic tech, and to research‑led roles where I can keep asking who, what, where, why, and who’s missing.
Having too many tabs open is my specialty

works.title: CYPHER

copy.brief: A uni assignment for Typography in Context: a magazine for visual communication designers, with masthead, covers and a style guide.
copy.insight: While organising my photographs into sections, I realised there was a cohesive colour scheme that heavily contrasted against the mundane urban landscape surrounding it.
copy.pull: Tags are acts of resistance to the increasing standardisation of urban environments.
copy.response: I colour-graded my photos and masked the backgrounds to enhance this contrast. One spot colour per spread gives the range of street art without clashing, on a grid deliberately broken in key moments, where imposed order coexists with graffiti.
copy.credit: Issue 5 cover artwork, which flows across the front and back cover. Made from my photographs and extended with Photoshop Generative Fill (Adobe Firefly). Graffiti belongs to its writers.

steps: ISSUE 5 · BACK COVER

The back cover continues the street scene from the front, with the masthead tag repeated in the orange spot colour above the issue blurb. The masthead is a chisel‑marker tag that changes every issue. For Issue 5 the E becomes an epsilon, the Greek numeral five.
STYLE GUIDE · 1.1 MASTHEAD · 3.2 LAYOUT · 4.1 BODY TEXT
I wrote a style guide that sets the rules for the masthead, type, grid and body text, so each issue can change its masthead and still read as CYPHER. Issue 5 is the reference for every rule.

works.title: 16 Days of Real Talk
works.context: Socially Responsive Design, UTS · with WAGEC via UTS Shopfront

copy.brief: A live client project for Socially Responsive Design at UTS. The Women’s and Girls’ Emergency Centre (WAGEC) asked our studio to launch its We Need To Talk cards to university students during the 16 Days of Activism against gender-based violence.
copy.pull: Almost half the students we surveyed had seen or experienced sexism at uni in the past year.
copy.response: We redesigned the deck as 30 pocket-sized cards, colour-coded by topic so students choose how deep to go. We used speech bubbles as the main device to show that not every opinion has to be fully formed to be part of the conversation.
copy.role: I worked on research and positioning, project management and the kickoff workshop, and designed and built the landing page in Webflow.
copy.credit: Printed cards. Card questions are by WAGEC. I set the card typography, shared the layout with Rachel, made the majority of the speech-bubble shapes and did the colours, textures and shadows. Teammates made the final artwork.

steps: OBSERVED · DECK TEST · W3
The original cards felt meaningful but too formal, large and academic, especially in a second language.
DECIDED
We made the cards smaller and type‑led, with clarity and readability as the priority.
TYPOGRAPHY · MINE

I set the card typography in Apercu Condensed and Work Sans, balancing clarity with warmth. I made the majority of the speech-bubble shapes and did the colours, textures and shadows. Teammates made the final artwork.
WEB · MINE

I designed the landing page, the campaign’s hub where students download the digital cards and find WAGEC resources. Ownership could not transfer, so WAGEC rebuilt it from my handover style guide and assets.
REELS · CREATIVE DIRECTION MINE
Student interviews paired with anonymous submissions, so students can take part safely.
POSTERS
By Angel, Helen, Seoyun & Nicole, using my type, shapes and textures. Campaign copy by Carmen, freelance copywriter.

works.title: Symbiosis
works.sub: Immersive installation concept for the Powerhouse Museum
works.context: Visualising Experience, UTS · Powerhouse Museum brief

copy.brief: A university assignment for Visualising Experience at UTS, working with the Powerhouse Museum collection: design an interactive digital experience for one object. I chose Christopher Dresser’s cast‑iron Garden Chair, 1870.
copy.insight: We see the chair as either a utilitarian object or a piece of art. Reading Dresser’s own books, I found that division reflects design for standardisation rather than an intrinsic truth, and that his ornament is built on botany and geometry.
copy.pull: Symbiosis is an immersive installation inspired by Dresser’s philosophy that true appreciation of beauty arises from contextual knowledge and understanding.
copy.response: It uses the Garden Chair to critique the arbitrary homogenisation of everyday objects. Visitors enter through mesh pathways with projections on the walls and floor, and symbols around the chair light up the principles hidden in its design.
copy.credit: FINAL VISUAL NARRATIVE · RENDERS & MODELS MY OWN

steps: 01 CONCEPT DEVELOPMENT · RESEARCH

I read two of Dresser’s books entirely through and traced the chair in Procreate. My first mind map needed constant reorganising, so I pulled out the figures he references in each chapter and made an annotated mind map of these instead, which allowed me to visually see the connections between ideas and concepts.
DECIDED

I decided to use modern technologies to reimagine Dresser’s ornamental imagery and engage a contemporary audience with the relationship between science, nature and the arts, creating an ethereal atmosphere without overpowering the concept itself.
CHRISTOPHER DRESSER

“We have here not only a manifestation of the truth that a principle of order prevails in the development of plants, but also a revelation of the fact that plants are founded upon a geometric basis.” Set in my final render around the chair.
02 CONCEPT 01 · VR USER JOURNEY
My initial design was a VR experience where the user could ‘pick up’ a floral motif from the chair and examine it closer.
CREATIVE CODE · WEEKS 5–6
I coded this gesture in p5.js with ml5 hand tracking and my own Teachable Machine classifier.
DECIDED
The classifier needed still images while the animation ran on live video, so I used ml5 hand tracking alone.
WHAT IT TAUGHT ME
Removing unnecessary complexity can lead to better performance.
03 CONCEPT 02 · REFINEMENT
A headset keeps the experience to one person, and studio feedback was to focus on the experience, not the technology.
DESIGN CONCEPT 02
I moved to projection mapping inside sheer walls, with light projected onto fabric so groups explore together.
PROTOTYPE 1 · MATERIALS
After a wide range of material experimentation, I selected the gutter guard for its structural integrity but adapted my approach due to sharp edges.
04 TESTING · PROTOTYPES 1–3
Did the structure guide visitors through at least 2 pathways, in and out?
PROTOTYPE 1 · SPATIAL EXPLORATION & NAVIGATION
A small-scale model to test how intuitive it is to navigate the pathways. I observed users without interference and recorded the paths they took to the centre.
PROTOTYPE 2 · INTERACTIVE LEARNING & CONCEPTUAL ENGAGEMENT
Tested whether the symbol interaction is intuitive and whether visitors can derive meaning independently. One user attempted to sit on the symbol, and two reached to touch it.
PROTOTYPE 3 · IMMERSIVE SENSORY EXPERIENCE
Assessed immersion through passive interaction with movement-tracked evolving projections and natural ambient sounds.
DECIDED · PROTOTYPE 2
Orientation was the primary requirement, with no ‘correct’ interaction.
WHAT IT TAUGHT ME
Prototype 2 taught me the necessity of clear interaction cues, and revealed how users interpret design elements in unexpected ways.
05 FINAL EXPERIENCE · WALKTHROUGH
I simulated tracking in testing by manually adjusting the projector, so the final concept uses automated motion tracking.
WHAT VISITORS TOOK AWAY · PROTOTYPE 3

Even without displaying the chair itself, the projections successfully conveyed the intended concepts. When asked what the projection was displaying, there was a unanimous understanding that by the end of the path, the visuals were communicating the geometric complexities behind the final shape.

works.title: IBM × QT Hotels

copy.brief: A uni assignment for Design Practice at UTS with IBM as industry partner: use Enterprise Design Thinking to help a hotel find the right problem to solve with AI. I worked on QT Hotels, where the question became how QT can leverage AI to enhance the check-in experience for business travellers while ensuring ROI.
copy.insight: Research and the as-is scenario mapping grouped guest pain points into three themes: personalisation & experience, digital & seamless processes, and corporate clashes over invoicing, tipping and compliance. Evaluating each for impact and feasibility pointed the workshop towards digital integration and seamless processes.
copy.response: Our agenda moved from an emoji icebreaker to an as-is scenario map of the check-in experience, then a prioritisation grid. In the playback I recommended digital integration first, and more research with QT guests and staff, because we didn’t get as many sponsor users as we would like.
copy.role: Team of 4. I designed the board system and agenda, co‑facilitated the workshop and presented the playback.
copy.credit: Workshop on Zoom and Miro. Research presentation in Figma Slides, playback deck in Canva.
copy.oneLine: An hour on Zoom and Miro with QT stakeholders, from front desk to CEO, to find where AI could help check-in.

works.title: COLLAB
works.context: Design Practice, UTS · Jack Morton brief for Figma

copy.brief: Jack Morton brief for Figma’s COLLAB event.
copy.insight: Research into Figma’s AI strategy found that AI had a big impact on individual work but very little on collaboration, while design trends were shifting away from stereotypical high-tech aesthetics towards more human-centred, approachable designs. The identity had to communicate AI as a helpful and friendly tool rather than a cold and intimidating force.
copy.response: I merged the playful, inflated letterforms of my first territory with the tactile, modular building blocks of my second, and imitated the wood and plastic textures of childhood toys for a sense of tactile nostalgia. The identity leads the stage concept, and the activation carries the same nostalgia through hands-on play, from a colouring station to clay moulding.
copy.credit: Identity explorations in Illustrator, presented in Figma Slides.
copy.oneLine: Play, Powered moves away from the high-tech look commonly associated with AI to show the childlike curiosity that emerges when AI handles the mundane routine tasks.

works.title: ADHD in the Media

copy.brief: A uni assignment for Contexts of Visual Communication at UTS: script and storyboard a 1-minute explainer video that applies a lens to a real-world issue. I took a feminist lens to gender bias in ADHD research and diagnosis.
copy.insight: Headlines blaming TikTok for the rise in ADHD diagnoses miss the deeply rooted biases in medical research and diagnosis. The study they cite examined content quality, not the platform’s role in diagnoses, while girls are still underdiagnosed and often treated for a mood disorder before their ADHD is recognised.
copy.response: I wrote the script and storyboarded it as a stop-motion newspaper collage, where the headline stamps on, the DSM timeline pans in from the right and text hand-writes on with the narration. It moves from a quick history lesson to the statistics and a myth-busting breakdown of the headline, and ends on a call to action: do not blame the inevitable downfall of a broken system on the individuals fighting to make it better.
copy.credit: Style frames in Adobe Express, presentation slides in Canva.
copy.oneLine: A feminist explainer on gender bias in ADHD research and diagnosis.

reviewFlags: The brief was script and storyboard only (‘You are not producing the explainer video’). works.title: Terms of Practice

copy.brief: A uni assignment for Research Through Design at UTS: critique existing design manifestos, then write and design my own. I analysed First Things First, Giorgia Lupi’s Data Humanism, Meta’s The Future is for Everyone and Mierle Laderman Ukeles’ Manifesto for Maintenance Art.
copy.insight: Re-reading them, I realised I’d been circling language in all of them: First Things First never says ‘you’, Lupi naturalises data as water, and on Meta I’d been fixing their words. Words are the smallest change a new designer controls, and they can have immense impacts, so language became the manifesto.
copy.response: I built a manifesto site where loaded industry terms like user, seamless and the cloud get struck and restored in place, plus a sourced word bank to take into your own work. Peers reviewed my first test draft as a design rather than using it, so the final leads in from a landing word field, splits manifesto and phrasebook into industry blue and restored yellow, and puts the summary first with notes on request.
copy.credit: I built my wireframe into the live site with AI.
copy.oneLine: A manifesto for digital experience designers entering an industry that speaks differently to the one that trained us.

works.title: Hand-tracking bloom

copy.brief: A uni assignment for Visualising Experience at UTS: an experiments folio across AR/VR, prototyping software and coding for interaction, alongside my Powerhouse Museum project.
copy.insight: My Teachable Machine classifier needed still images while the animation ran on live video, so the two models could not run together.
copy.response: I dropped the classifier and used the ml5 wrist and fingertip key points for gestural control, which also opened up scaling and rotation across more than one axis.
copy.credit: p5.js, ml5 hand tracking and Google Teachable Machine. Built from the ml5 hand tracking example provided in class.
copy.oneLine: A flower pinned to the open hand, coded in p5.js with ml5 hand tracking, that blooms as the hand opens and shrinks and glows as it closes.

copy.brief: A live client project for Socially Responsive Design at UTS: WAGEC asked our studio to launch its We Need To Talk cards to university students during the 16 Days of Activism against gender-based violence.
copy.insight: A survey of 40 students showed they valued anonymity and the chance to share without fear of backlash, which pointed us to type-based and distorted visuals that protect identity.
copy.response: We proposed three creative territories for the cards, from simple type-led prompts to illustrated scenes and a playful levels-of-depth concept.
copy.role: Team of 6 (Asterisk Studios). I wrote the audience and competitor analysis, the additional secondary research, the purpose statement and the comparison of the three directions, and planned the structure and scripts for the client kickoff workshop.
copy.credit: Student survey by Helen, immersive testing and interviews by Nicole, concept mapping by Seoyun, moodboards by Angel and thumbnail sketches by Rachel.
copy.oneLine: Our reverse brief and design strategy for WAGEC's We Need To Talk cards during the 16 Days of Activism, ending in three creative territories for the campaign.

works.title: Trust in Transition

copy.brief: A uni assignment for UX Design at UTS: a research folio on how UX design can address the trust deficit in the energy transition.
copy.insight: Mapping stakeholders, root causes and personas showed that social and behavioural barriers outweigh technical and economic ones, and that trust, accessibility and autonomy hold back people who want to act.
copy.response: I proposed a community-driven platform that connects local action to wider movements and gives communities a democratic voice in energy decisions.
copy.credit: Stakeholder map started as an in-class group brainstorm, which I refined on my own. Personas drew on informal interviews with family and friends.
copy.oneLine: A UX research folio on the trust deficit between energy transition initiatives and climate advocates, ending in a proposal for a community-driven platform.

works.title: What’s your excuse?

works.title: Beneath the Beauty

copy.brief: A uni assignment for Narrative, Form & Time (Sprint 1, Video Design): a video responding to an article by Dr Zoe Sadokierski & Ceridwen Dovey on Dr Claire Rowe's research into upside-down jellyfish.
copy.insight: A contrasting word list showed the article's narrative moving from beauty and mystery to chaos and destruction, and that progression became the structure of the video.
copy.response: I filmed jellyfish at the aquarium and urban scenes for part 2, then built tension from serene music, elegant type and vibrant footage to chaotic typography, darker less saturated tones and overstimulating layers of sound.
copy.credit: Edited in After Effects. Footage filmed by me at the aquarium and in urban settings.
copy.oneLine: A short video that follows upside-down jellyfish from beautiful marine life to human-facilitated ecosystem invaders, told through compositing, colour grading and sound.

works.title: Jellyfish Genesis: A Celestial Hypothesis

copy.brief: A uni assignment for Narrative, Form & Time (Sprint 2, Graphic Narrative), inspired by 'Survival Stories - Meet the Scientist: Dr Claire Rowe' by Dr Zoe Sadokierski & Ceridwen Dovey.
copy.insight: The article's uncanny themes and the jellyfish's links to Greek mythology, the constellation Cassiopeia and its star Cassiopeia A became my own interpretation, a new way to look at the creatures.
copy.response: After script feedback I opened with a personal anecdote of me researching at my desk and set the cosmic origin story as the second part, drawn as digital illustrations after learning perspective grids, anatomy and expressions.
copy.oneLine: A digital graphic narrative that links the mysterious origins of upside-down jellyfish to the Cassiopeia constellation and a star exploding.

works.title: Nomad Homes

copy.brief: A group assignment for Design Futuring (AT2): a future storyworld shown through a presentation, a group written submission and individual diegetic prototypes.
copy.insight: Researching the government's response to the 2022 floods, I found many families felt isolated living in makeshift accommodation that lacked a sense of home, so the mobile home prioritises a homely atmosphere and community.
copy.response: I designed the mobile home itself, with wood and earth tones and curved forms, retractable wheels so it reads as permanent when parked, roof shelters that link homes into communal spaces, and a hydrogen-producing solar paint to power it.
copy.role: Team of 5. I researched the government's response to the 2022 floods and produced the research and visualisations for the overall mobile home design and its material technologies.
copy.credit: With Allaine Villanueva (synopsis, resource kit), Xinyue (Cindy) Zhang (Acknowledgement of Country, critical rationale, navigation app), Ruby Brook (present-day world, water management) and Alice Qin (personas, past world, bioluminescent plants).
copy.oneLine: A speculative 2064 where flooding has pushed NSW coastal communities inland into government-issued mobile homes, told through a storyworld and diegetic prototypes.

works.title: My life is very slow

copy.brief: A uni assignment for Narrative, Form & Time (Sprint 3, Motion Design): a motion sequence using a sentence from Dr Rowe's voice recordings for the same article.
copy.insight: Rereading the article and listening to the voiceover again, I noticed a motif of gentle currents and how they interplay with the jellyfish, so I focused on a sense of calm and fluidity.
copy.response: I set at least one new goal or constraint each week, built the water material in WOMP and kept the animation to camera movement, then slowed the voiceover to 0.8 speed with slight echo and reverb.
copy.credit: Materials and renders in WOMP. Blender physics simulations tested in process, not used in the final.
copy.oneLine: A 3D motion sequence where the camera flows through water drops to share the slow, calm life of an upside-down jellyfish, set to Dr Claire Rowe's voiceover.

works.title: Materials & Process

copy.brief: A uni assignment for Politics of Image & Text (Task 2): a folio answering 3 workshop briefs in collage, documentary-style photography and grid & type.
copy.insight: Research into music's role in relationships led to thread as the motif holding fragmented images of couples together, and Trent Parke's 'White Man' led me to look for the extraordinary in the midst of the ordinary.
copy.response: I threaded 8 collage stickers by hand and photographed them under raised LED light, restaged Parke's photograph as an empty, sunlit chair and table in building 8, and set Margaret Atwood's 'Tracking the Rain' as 9 Instagram stories that move from neon cyber-green to an earth-toned green.
copy.credit: Collages use found imagery: black and white images of couples from old movies found in the studio paper bin, magazine cut-outs, and images of Audrey Hepburn and Madonna. Photograph reimagines 'White Man' from Minutes to Midnight by Trent Parke. Poem 'Tracking the Rain' by Margaret Atwood. Edited in Lightroom and Photoshop, type set in Acumin Pro, sketches in Procreate, radar graphics in Illustrator.
copy.oneLine: A folio of 3 workshop briefs: hand-threaded collage stickers about music holding people together, a Trent Parke re-staging and a typographic Instagram story series.
